There's the logic behind it that is essential to understanding.

Von Neumann had a solution to a biased coin. Toss the coin twice, if it lands on the same thing twice in a row, discard the results and start over. If it doesn't land on the same thing twice in a row, take the result of the first toss.
That would automatically favor the opposite side of the favored side, no? After all, the favored side being flipped twoce is more probable than the obverse.

But, wouldn't that only be an issue if you counted the other side twice in a row? I don't see how the bias would effect the order of two non-matching tosses.

So if we get: HH we ignore it and toss again, this would cause a bias if we counted TT, but we don't.

The only results we accept are: HT and TH, neither should have an advantage.

If the tendency is H then HH is also the tendency and HHH is less likely than HHT because of distributions. So, we've not really solved it, just made it slightly more fair. The odds of HHH are lower than the odds of HHT. Instead of a 51% bias, it may reduce it to 50.5%, though I've not done the math.

In the grand scheme of things, it's probably close enough.

Oh, I guess I should have been more specific. We'll never record the last two results of three tosses. If we get HH or TT, we start over and do two more flips. Of course, there would be a sleight possibility that we'd be repeating it forever, but that case is so small it's not worth worrying about.
